title: Nested Crates
statement: A mover stores crates inside one another to save space. Each crate is [width, height] (no rotation allowed), and crate A fits inside crate B only if A is strictly narrower and strictly shorter than B. Return the largest number of crates that can be nested in a single chain.

examples.explanation: Identical crates cannot nest: one crate.

hints.content: Sort by width so a chain only ever moves forward in the list.
After sorting, you need the longest strictly increasing run of heights, which is a longest increasing subsequence.
Crates with equal widths cannot nest, but a plain LIS on heights might chain them.
Break width ties by sorting heights in decreasing order, so two crates of the same width can never both appear in an increasing subsequence.
Then run the O(n log n) LIS: keep the smallest possible tail height for each chain length and binary search where each height fits.

testCases.explanation: Identical crates cannot nest: one crate.
Wider crates are shorter, so no two nest.
Equal widths cannot nest even when heights increase.
Ties in width require care when ordering.
Many crates where the quadratic chain search is slow.

solutions.title: Quadratic chain DP
solutions.intuition: After sorting by width, the longest chain ending at a crate extends the best chain ending at any crate that fits inside it.
solutions.approach: Sort by width. chain[i] = 1 + max chain[j] over j < i with strictly smaller width and height. Return the maximum.
solutions.pseudocode: sort by width; for i: chain[i] = 1 + max(chain[j] for j < i if w[j] < w[i] and h[j] < h[i]); return max
commonMistakes: Checking only heights and allowing equal widths to nest.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Sorting reduces nesting to a chain DP, but comparing every pair is quadratic.

solutions.title: Sort with a tie-break, then LIS in n log n
solutions.intuition: Sorting widths ascending with heights descending among equal widths turns nesting into a strictly increasing subsequence on heights alone.
solutions.approach: Sort by width ascending, then height descending. Maintain tails: for each height, binary search the first tail >= height and replace it (or append). The tails length is the answer.
commonMistakes: Sorting equal widths by ascending height, which lets same-width crates chain.
Using an upper bound (<= h), which allows equal heights to nest.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the Russian-doll pattern: sort by width, and break width ties by descending height so same-width crates can't both be chosen. Nesting then becomes a strictly increasing subsequence of heights, solved in O(n log n) with the smallest-tails array and a lower-bound binary search.
